pos: adj. (having the hoof divided into two parts; one of the two marks of a clean beast under the law)
etymology: From cloven, the old past participle of cleave, to split, and foot. The Authorized Version renders the Hebrew phrase for a hoof wholly parted into two.
biblical_def: The dietary law of Leviticus 11 turns on two marks in a beast, and both are required: “Whatsoever parteth the hoof, and is clovenfooted, and cheweth the cud, among the beasts, that shall ye eat” (Lev 11:3). One mark alone will not do. The camel chews the cud and does not divide the hoof; the swine divides the hoof and is clovenfooted and does not chew the cud, “he is unclean to you” (Lev 11:7). The carcase of any beast not clovenfooted defiles the man who touches it (Lev 11:26). The Reformed tradition has long read the two marks as a parable in the flesh: the parted hoof is the separated walk, the outward life visibly distinguished from the world; the chewing of the cud is inward meditation, the word taken in and brought up again and ruminated. A beast with the walk and no meditation is a swine; a beast with meditation and no separated walk is a camel; and the law will accept neither. Whether or not every detail of that reading is pressed, the law itself teaches Israel to be a people marked out at the table three times a day, and Peter's sheet in Acts 10 is the moment the marking-out was declared fulfilled and the middle wall broken down.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines clovenfooted as having the foot or hoof divided into two parts, as the ox; also written cloven-hoofed.
webster_full: CLOVEN-FOOTED, CLOVEN-HOOFED, a. Having the foot or hoof divided into two parts, as the ox.
CLOVEN, pp. of cleave. Divided; parted; split.
In Scripture, the dividing of the hoof was one of the marks of a clean beast, joined with the chewing of the cud.
scriptures: Lev 11:7
And the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you.
Deu 14:6
And every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat.
And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
corruption_summary: The dietary law is either dismissed as primitive food-superstition or re-imposed on Christians as a health code, and both readings miss what Leviticus itself says it was for: to teach a people to be separate.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet over this law. The first treats Leviticus 11 as ancient hygiene — a bronze-age food code about trichinosis and shellfish — and so reduces the holiness of God to a public-health measure. Leviticus gives its own reason, and it is not medical: ye shall be holy; for I am holy (Lev 11:44-45). The marks on the beast were a daily catechism in separateness, taught at every meal to a people surrounded by nations who ate everything. The second error runs the other way and re-imposes the code on the church as a rule of Christian obedience or Christian health. Peter's vision answers it: what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common (Act 10:15), and Mark records the Lord's own verdict that He was purging all meats (Mar 7:19). Paul forbids any man to judge a brother in meat or in drink, calling these things a shadow of things to come, but the body is of Christ (Col 2:16-17). The shadow is not despised; it is fulfilled. And the substance abides: a people marked out, visibly distinguished, holy unto the LORD — no longer at the table, but in the whole walk.
roots_summary: Hebrew parac parcah, to divide the hoof; shaca' (H8156), to cleave or split, of the hoof cleft into two claws; parcah (H6541), a hoof.
roots_lines: Hebrew parcah (H6541) — a hoof, a claw; the divided hoof is the first mark of a clean beast; Leviticus 11:3, Deuteronomy 14:6.
Hebrew shaca' (H8156) — to cleave, to split; the cleft parted into two claws; Deuteronomy 14:6, Leviticus 11:7.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, and so ceremonially unclean; the word of Peter's protest and of the voice that answered him; Acts 10:14-15.
usage: “Parteth the hoof, and is clovenfooted, and cheweth the cud” — both marks required, never one.
“The swine…is unclean to you” — the walk without the meditation.
“What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” — the shadow fulfilled at Joppa.

pos: v. (to grind with the teeth; in the law, to chew the cud, the second mark of a clean beast)
etymology: Old English ceowan, to chew. The Hebrew idiom of Leviticus 11 is literally “to bring up the cud” — the beast returns the food to the mouth and works it again.
biblical_def: “Nevertheless these shall ye not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the hoof: as the camel, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you” (Lev 11:4). Moses repeats the law in Deuteronomy with the camel, the hare, and the coney named: “for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof; therefore they are unclean unto you” (Deu 14:7). To chew the cud is to bring the food up from the stomach and grind it again — the beast eats its meal twice, and slowly. The old expositors, from the fathers through the Puritans, took it as the natural emblem of meditation on the word: not the swift reading that swallows a chapter whole, but the returning to it, the working of it over until the sweetness is out. Psalm 1 says the blessed man's delight is in the law of the LORD, and in his law doth he meditate day and night; Joshua is told the book shall not depart out of his mouth. The camel is the warning attached: a beast may ruminate all day and still be unclean, because meditation without a separated walk is not obedience. Both marks, or neither.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to chew as to bite and grind with the teeth; to masticate; and figuratively, to ruminate in the thoughts; to meditate.
webster_full: CHEW, v.t. To bite and grind with the teeth; to masticate, as food, to prepare it for deglutition and digestion.
2. To ruminate in the thoughts; to meditate; as, to chew revenge.
3. To champ; to bite, hold or roll about in the mouth; as, to chew tobacco.
scriptures: Lev 11:4
Nevertheless these shall ye not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the hoof: as the camel, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you.
Deu 14:7

Nevertheless these ye shall not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the cloven hoof; as the camel, and the hare, and the coney: for they chew the cud, but divide not the hoof; therefore they are unclean unto you.
Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
corruption_summary: Reading has replaced ruminating: a generation with more Bible text available than any before it consumes chapters at speed and works none of them over, and calls the volume devotion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is plain and no one disputes it. What has been lost is the practice the clean beast pictures. The believer of 1650 might own one Bible, hear two sermons, and turn a single verse over for a week; the believer of today can carry every translation ever made in one hand, and the ordinary result is not depth but speed. Chewing the cud is a slow, repetitive, unglamorous business. It is reading the same paragraph on Tuesday that was read on Monday, and finding what Monday missed; it is carrying one clause into the workday and returning to it at noon; it is the psalmist's day and night. Meditation in the biblical sense has nothing to do with emptying the mind, which is the eastern practice that has borrowed the English word; it is filling the mind with a text and working it. The principle to recover is Joshua 1:8, where the promise of prosperity and good success is attached not to reading the book but to meditating therein day and night, and then doing according to all that is written.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'alah gerah, to bring up the cud; gerah (H1625), the cud; Hebrew hagah (H1897), to murmur, to muse, to meditate — the word of Psalm 1:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew gerah (H1625) — the cud; literally that which is brought up again and ground a second time; Leviticus 11:3-7, Deuteronomy 14:6-8.
Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to murmur, to mutter, to muse; the blessed man's meditation, spoken low and continually; Psalm 1:2, Joshua 1:8.
Hebrew siyach (H7878) — to ponder, to converse with oneself; the psalmist meditating in the night watches; Psalm 119:15, 63:6.
usage: “Because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof” — the camel, unclean for want of the second mark.
“They chew the cud, but divide not the hoof” — the camel, the hare, and the coney together.
“In his law doth he meditate day and night” — the practice the clean beast pictures.

pos: n. pl. (the membranous organs by which a fish swims; with scales, the two marks of a clean water creature)
etymology: Old English finn. The law of the waters is framed on two visible marks, exactly parallel to the two marks of the clean beast on land.
biblical_def: “These shall ye eat of all that are in the waters: whatsoever hath fins and scales in the waters, in the seas, and in the rivers, them shall ye eat” (Lev 11:9). What lacks them is not merely inedible but an abomination: “Whatsoever hath no fins nor scales in the waters, that shall be an abomination unto you” (Lev 11:12), and Deuteronomy repeats the rule for the whole nation (Deu 14:9-10). The two marks are again a pair, and again visible from outside. The fin is the organ of self-direction — the creature that has fins can move against the current instead of being carried by it; the scale is the covering, the armour that keeps the water out. The bottom-feeder that has neither goes where the water takes it and has nothing between itself and its element. Whether the expositors press the emblem or not, the structure of the law is unmistakable: on land, a parted hoof and a chewed cud; in the water, a fin and a scale; in the air, a list of birds that do not feed on carrion. Israel was to see holiness everywhere she looked, because holiness is what her God is, and every meal was a lesson in it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fin as the organ by which fishes balance themselves and direct their motions in the water; an oar-like member on the body of a fish.
webster_full: FIN, n. The organ by which fishes balance themselves and direct their motions in the water.
2. Fins are of several kinds; the dorsal, the pectoral, the ventral, the anal and the caudal.
By the Mosaic law, no fish was to be eaten which had not fins and scales.
scriptures: Lev 11:9
These shall ye eat of all that are in the waters: whatsoever hath fins and scales in the waters, in the seas, and in the rivers, them shall ye eat.
Whatsoever hath no fins nor scales in the waters, that shall be an abomination unto you.
And whatsoever hath not fins and scales ye may not eat; it is unclean unto you.
corruption_summary: The creature that cannot swim against the current is the picture of the age: a people formed entirely by whatever is presently moving, with no organ of resistance and no covering.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody disputes what a fin is. The principle to recover is the one the law makes visible. A fish with fins can hold its place in a moving river; a fish without them is where the current has put it, and its position tells you nothing about the fish and everything about the water. That is a fair description of a great deal of contemporary religion, in which convictions arrive and depart with the surrounding culture on a lag of about ten years, and each new position is announced as a fresh discovery of what the Bible always meant. Romans 12:2 is the fin: be not conformed to this world, but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind. The scale is the second half of the pair — the covering, the armour, and Ephesians 6 supplies it piece by piece. The law of the waters is not binding on the Christian's table; the pattern it teaches is binding on his life, because the God who wrote both is the same, and He is holy.
roots_summary: Hebrew c'nappiyr (H5579), a fin; qasqeseth (H7193), a scale; sheqets (H8263), a detestable thing, an abomination.
roots_lines: Hebrew c'nappiyr (H5579) — a fin; used only in the dietary law of the waters; Leviticus 11:9-12, Deuteronomy 14:9-10.
Hebrew qasqeseth (H7193) — a scale, of a fish or of armour; the same word is used of Goliath's coat of mail; Leviticus 11:9, 1 Samuel 17:5.
Hebrew sheqets (H8263) — a detestable thing, an abomination; the verdict on the finless creature; Leviticus 11:10-12.
usage: “Whatsoever hath fins and scales…them shall ye eat” — the two marks of the waters.
“That shall be an abomination unto you” — the creature with neither organ nor covering.
“It is unclean unto you” — Moses repeating the rule for the whole nation.

pos: adj. (not washed; the archaic past participle of wash, used of hands not ritually cleansed)
etymology: Old English un- and the strong past participle wæscen. The Authorized Version keeps the old strong form; modern English has flattened it to unwashed.
biblical_def: The word belongs to one controversy and one verdict. The Pharisees and scribes came from Jerusalem and “saw some of his disciples eat bread with defiled, that is to say, with unwashen, hands, they found fault” (Mar 7:2). Mark, writing for Gentiles, explains at length that the elders held a tradition of washing, and the charge was framed as a question: “Why walk not thy disciples according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with unwashen hands?” (Mar 7:5). This was not the ceremonial law of Moses. Moses commanded the priests to wash at the laver before ministering; he never commanded Israel to wash before ordinary bread. The rule was tradition, grown up around the law and then set above it. The Lord's answer went to the heart of the matter: ye lay aside the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition — and He instanced Corban, the vow by which a man could starve his own parents while appearing devout. Then His verdict, plainly stated: “These are the things which defile a man: but to eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man” (Mat 15:20). Defilement is from within, out of the heart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unwashen as not washed; not cleansed by water — an obsolete form retained in the Scriptures.
webster_full: UNWASHEN, a. Not washed; not cleansed by water.
To eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man. Matt. xv.
UNWASHED, a. Not washed; filthy.
scriptures: These are the things which defile a man: but to eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man.
Mar 7:5
Then the Pharisees and scribes asked him, Why walk not thy disciples according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with unwashen hands?
Mar 7:8
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do.
corruption_summary: Every generation grows its own unwritten washings and defends them as though they were the law of God, and the church polices the traditions it invented while the commandments of God go unkept.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 7 is the definitive New Testament text on man-made religious rule, and its mechanism is worth watching closely, because it is not stupidity and it is not hypocrisy in the crude sense. The washing of hands began as a genuine act of reverence, an extension of priestly practice to ordinary life; it became a fence around the law; the fence became a test of fellowship; and at last the fence was defended more energetically than the law it was built to protect. That sequence repeats in every century, and the traditions differ only in content. Reformed and Baptist churches are not exempt; they have their own unwritten washings, defended with the heat proper to Scripture and found nowhere in it. The Lord gives two tests. The first: does the tradition, in practice, set aside a commandment of God, as Corban set aside Honour thy father and thy mother? The second is the deeper one and it is in Matthew 15:20 — He does not merely relax the rule, He relocates defilement altogether. Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries. A man may keep every washing his church has invented and be filthy; the regulative principle of worship, rightly held, is precisely the protection against this, because it binds the church to what God has commanded and forbids the imposition of what He has not.
roots_summary: Greek aniptos (G449), unwashed; koinos (G2839), common, defiled; paradosis (G3862), a tradition, that which is handed down.
roots_lines: Greek aniptos (G449) — unwashed, of hands not ceremonially rinsed; Matthew 15:20, Mark 7:2, 7:5.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, and so profane or defiled; Mark glosses unwashen with it for his Gentile readers; Mark 7:2, Acts 10:14.
Greek paradosis (G3862) — a tradition, that which is handed over; condemned when of men, commanded when apostolic; Mark 7:8, 2 Thessalonians 2:15.
usage: “Eat bread with unwashen hands” — the charge that revealed the accusers.
“To eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man” — the verdict that relocated defilement to the heart.
“Laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men” — the mechanism named.

pos: adj. (in the state of ceremonial separation appointed for a woman in Leviticus 15; used figuratively of what is set apart as defiled)
etymology: Latin menstruus, monthly, from mensis, a month. The Authorized Version uses the plain medical adjective of the day, always with a ceremonial rather than a moral force in the law itself.
biblical_def: The law of Leviticus 15 appointed a season of ceremonial separation, and Scripture treats it as a matter of ritual purity, not of sin: the woman was not guilty, she was set apart, and the same chapter appoints a like separation for the man. The prophets then take the image and use it for what is unfit to come near God. Isaiah promises a day when the idols will be so hated that Israel will cast the silver and gold from her images away “as a menstruous cloth” and say unto it, Get thee hence (Isa 30:22) — the very metal that had been worshipped handled as something to be got rid of. Jeremiah's lament: “Jerusalem is as a menstruous woman among them” (Lam 1:17), the holy city put outside the camp. Ezekiel lists it among the marks of the just man that he hath not come near to a menstruous woman (Eze 18:6), that is, he keeps the law where the law separates. And Isaiah 64:6 takes the same imagery to its deepest point: all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags. That is the doctrine of total depravity in a domestic figure — not our sins but our righteousnesses, the best we have, unfit to be brought near.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines menstruous as having the monthly flow or discharge; pertaining to the monthly courses of females.
webster_full: MENSTRUOUS, a. Having the monthly flow or discharge; pertaining to the monthly courses of females.
2. Pertaining to a menstruum.
In Scripture, used figuratively of that which is set apart as unclean and cast away with loathing.
scriptures: Ye shall defile also the covering of thy graven images of silver, and the ornament of thy molten images of gold: thou shalt cast them away as a menstruous cloth; thou shalt say unto it, Get thee hence.
Lam 1:17

Zion spreadeth forth her hands, and there is none to comfort her: the LORD hath commanded concerning Jacob, that his adversaries should be round about him: Jerusalem is as a menstruous woman among them.
Isa 64:6
But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away.
corruption_summary: The ceremonial separations of Leviticus 15 are read as a verdict on women, which the text does not say; and the prophets' use of the image is softened away from the doctrine it teaches.
corruption_paragraphs: Two things are commonly said about this law, and both are wrong. The first is that Leviticus 15 shames women as inherently defiling. The chapter is symmetrical: it legislates a bodily issue in the man in the first half and in the woman in the second, and in neither case is a sin-offering required for the ordinary condition, because no sin has been committed. Uncleanness in Leviticus is a category of nearness to the sanctuary, not of guilt, and the same chapter makes a man unclean for touching a bed. The whole apparatus taught one lesson — that fallen, mortal flesh cannot simply walk into the presence of a holy God — and it taught it through the ordinary facts of the body precisely so that no Israelite could forget it for a week. The second error runs opposite, and it belongs to the pulpit: preachers embarrassed by Isaiah 64:6 soften the image until the verse means our sins are unacceptable to God, which nobody disputes and which is not what Isaiah wrote. He wrote our righteousnesses. The best works of the best day of the best man, offered as a ground of acceptance, are what the prophet calls the filthy rag. That is why justification must be by an imputed righteousness not our own, and it is the sharpest verse in the Old Testament against every scheme of salvation by works.
roots_summary: Hebrew niddah (H5079), separation, the ceremonial removal of Leviticus 15; 'iddim, the word behind “filthy rags” in Isaiah 64:6; tame' (H2930), to be unclean.
roots_lines: Hebrew niddah (H5079) — separation, impurity; the noun for the appointed removal, and used by the prophets for what is cast away; Leviticus 15:19, Lamentations 1:17.
Hebrew 'iddim — the plural noun rendered “filthy rags”, a garment of the separation; Isaiah 64:6.
Hebrew tame' (H2930) — to be or become unclean; the great verb of the purity code, always about nearness to the sanctuary; Leviticus 11:24, 15:2.
usage: “Cast them away as a menstruous cloth” — the gold of the idols handled as refuse.
“Jerusalem is as a menstruous woman among them” — the holy city put outside the camp.
“All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags” — not our sins; our righteousnesses.

pos: n. (the marital act; in Leviticus, the phrase “seed of copulation” naming the occasion of a ceremonial washing)
etymology: Latin copulatio, a joining together, from copula, a bond or tie. The word in the Authorized Version is a plain and unembarrassed legal term.
biblical_def: Leviticus 15 legislates soberly and without shame: “if any man's seed of copulation go out from him, then he shall wash all his flesh in water, and be unclean until the even” (Lev 15:16); the garment likewise is washed (Lev 15:17); and “the woman also with whom man shall lie with seed of copulation, they shall both bathe themselves in water, and be unclean until the even” (Lev 15:18). Two things must be held together here or the passage is misread. First, the marital act is not sin. Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled (Heb 13:4); the command to be fruitful and multiply came before the fall; the Song of Solomon is in the canon; and Paul commands husbands and wives not to defraud one another. Second, in Israel even the good and God-given became an occasion of ceremonial uncleanness until evening, because the whole purity system was teaching one lesson relentlessly: the flesh, in its ordinary and lawful workings, is not the ground of access to a holy God. The washing was not a penance. It was a picture, and the water pointed forward to the washing of regeneration and the blood that alone gives boldness to enter the holiest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines copulation as the act of coupling; the coming together of male and female in generation; and generally, a joining together.
webster_full: COPULATION, n. The act of coupling or joining; union; conjunction.
2. The embrace of the sexes in generation.
COPULATE, v.i. To unite in sexual embrace, applied to the animal creation generally.
scriptures: And if any man's seed of copulation go out from him, then he shall wash all his flesh in water, and be unclean until the even.
The woman also with whom man shall lie with seed of copulation, they shall both bathe themselves in water, and be unclean until the even.
Heb 13:4
Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.
corruption_summary: Two ancient errors keep returning: the ascetic reading that treats the marriage bed itself as defiling, and the modern reading that treats the body as morally weightless — and Leviticus 15 with Hebrews 13:4 refutes both.
corruption_paragraphs: The ascetic error is the older. It reads the washings of Leviticus 15 as evidence that the marital act is intrinsically polluting, and it produced in the medieval church a whole apparatus of enforced clerical celibacy, of marriage graded beneath virginity, and of penitential rules governing the marriage bed by the church calendar. Paul had already named that teaching for what it is: forbidding to marry is a doctrine of devils (1Ti 4:1-3), and the Reformers recovered the honour of marriage precisely by preaching Hebrews 13:4. Leviticus never called the act sinful; it required no sin-offering, only water and the passing of a day. The opposite error is the one now in possession, and it is not asceticism but weightlessness: the body treated as an instrument for pleasure carrying no covenant meaning at all, so that what is done with it is held to signify nothing about the soul. Paul answers that with the strongest argument he has, and it is not a rule but a doctrine: know ye not that your bodies are the members of Christ? The body is for the Lord, and the Lord for the body (1Co 6:13-15). Between the two errors stands the biblical account — the marriage bed honourable and undefiled, guarded by a covenant, and the flesh, even at its most lawful, never the ground of access to God.
roots_summary: Hebrew shikbath zera', an emission of seed, the literal phrase behind “seed of copulation”; rachats (H7364), to wash or bathe; Greek koite (G2845), the bed, whence Hebrews 13:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew shikbath zera' — literally a lying-down of seed; the legal phrase of Leviticus 15; Leviticus 15:16-18.
Hebrew rachats (H7364) — to wash, to bathe the whole body; the prescribed remedy, and the word of Naaman's washing in Jordan; Leviticus 15:16, 2 Kings 5:10.
Greek koite (G2845) — a bed, and by metonymy the marriage bed; declared undefiled, with a warning attached; Hebrews 13:4.
usage: “He shall wash all his flesh in water, and be unclean until the even” — a washing, not a penance.
“They both bathe themselves in water” — the law legislating alike for husband and wife.
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” — the New Testament verdict.

pos: n. (saliva; the moisture of the mouth)
etymology: Old English spatl, saliva, related to spittan, to spit. A word of contempt in the ancient world, and therefore the more remarkable in the hands of Christ.
biblical_def: Three scenes, and the movement between them is the gospel in miniature. David, in danger at Gath, “feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard” (1Sa 21:13) — the LORD's anointed drooling in a Philistine gateway to escape with his life, and the psalm that came out of that day is Psalm 34: I sought the LORD, and he heard me. Job, in his extremity, asks God for the space of a swallow: “How long wilt thou not depart from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle?” (Job 7:19) — a man too pressed to have a moment to himself. Then the Lord Jesus at Siloam: “he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay” (Joh 9:6). He who was Himself spit upon in the judgment hall took the most contemptible substance and made it the instrument of sight; He made clay, as at the beginning He formed man of the dust of the ground, and the man born blind received eyes that had never existed. Isaiah had prophesied both halves: I hid not my face from shame and spitting.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines spittle as the thick moist substance secreted by the salivary glands; saliva.
webster_full: SPITTLE, n. The thick moist matter which is secreted by the salivary glands; saliva.
2. A small sort of spade.
SPIT, v.t. To eject from the mouth; to throw out, as saliva or other matter.
scriptures: And he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard.
Joh 9:6
When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay,
Isa 50:6
I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting.
corruption_summary: John 9 is regularly reduced to a healing anecdote, and its actual subject — that the man born blind was blind so that the works of God should be made manifest in him — is precisely the answer our age refuses to hear.
corruption_paragraphs: The disciples asked the question our age still asks, and asked it in the old form: Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? The Lord's answer refuses both options and gives a third: neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him (Joh 9:3). A man was born without sight, lived a lifetime begging, and the reason given by the Lord Himself is that God intended to be glorified in him on a particular day. That answer is intolerable to a therapeutic account of suffering, which requires that affliction be either explained as someone's fault or dissolved as meaningless; and it is intolerable to the prosperity teaching, which requires that no believer be born blind at all. Scripture gives a harder and better answer. The affliction was real, lifelong, and appointed; it was not punishment; and it had a purpose the sufferer could not have known until the day the clay was laid on his eyes. The same chapter shows what he did with it: cast out of the synagogue, he worshipped Christ, and gave the plainest testimony in the Gospels — one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see.
roots_summary: Hebrew riyr (H7388), spittle, saliva; Greek ptusma (G4427), spittle; ptuo (G4429), to spit; emptuo (G1716), to spit upon, of the mockers at the passion.
roots_lines: Hebrew riyr (H7388) — spittle, or the white of an egg; used of David's feigned madness at Gath; 1 Samuel 21:13, Job 6:6.
Greek ptusma (G4427) — spittle; used only of the clay the Lord made at Siloam; John 9:6.
Greek emptuo (G1716) — to spit upon; the mockery of the Sanhedrin and of the soldiers, foretold in Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 26:67, Mark 15:19.
usage: “Let his spittle fall down upon his beard” — the anointed of the LORD feigning madness at Gath.
“Made clay of the spittle” — the despised substance made the instrument of sight.
“I hid not my face from shame and spitting” — the Servant foretold.

pos: adj. (boiled; the archaic past participle of seethe)
etymology: Old English soden, past participle of seothan, to seethe or boil. Modern English has kept the word only in its secondary sense of saturated; the Authorized Version uses it in the plain original.
biblical_def: The word is a fixed point in the law of the passover: “Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire; his head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof” (Exo 12:9). The lamb was to go whole into the fire, not be jointed into a pot, and not a bone of him was to be broken — a command John cites at the cross as fulfilled prophecy. Boiling divides and disperses; roasting keeps the victim entire and puts it through the fire. It appears again in the law of the sin offering, where the earthen vessel in which the flesh is sodden must be broken, and a brasen pot scoured and rinsed (Lev 6:28), because what has touched the holy thing cannot simply return to common use. The Nazarite's peace offering included “the sodden shoulder of the ram” (Num 6:19). And Eli's sons overturned the whole order at Shiloh, demanding raw flesh before the fat was burnt: “he will not have sodden flesh of thee, but raw” (1Sa 2:15) — priests who would not wait for God's portion to go up first. The most terrible use is Lamentations 4:10, the siege that drove the pitiful women to seethe their own children.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sodden as boiled; seethed; the participle passive of seethe.
webster_full: SODDEN, pp. of seethe. Boiled; decocted.
SEETHE, v.t. To boil; to decoct or prepare for food in hot liquor.
Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire. Ex. xii.
scriptures: Exo 12:9
Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire; his head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof.
Lev 6:28
But the earthen vessel wherein it is sodden shall be broken: and if it be sodden in a brasen pot, it shall be both scoured, and rinsed in water.
Also before they burnt the fat, the priest's servant came, and said to the man that sacrificed, Give flesh to roast for the priest; for he will not have sodden flesh of thee, but raw.
corruption_summary: The precision of the passover instructions is treated as arbitrary ritual detail, when the New Testament makes at least one of those details — the unbroken bones of the lamb — a prophecy fulfilled at the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No one is contesting the meaning of sodden. The principle to recover is that the details of the passover were not arbitrary, and Scripture proves it by picking one of them up centuries later. The lamb was to be roast with fire and not sodden, eaten whole, and not a bone of it broken (Exo 12:46). At Golgotha the soldiers came to break the legs of the crucified to hasten death; they broke the legs of the two thieves; and when they came to Jesus and saw He was dead already, they brake not His legs. John stops the narrative to say why: these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken (Joh 19:36). A regulation about cookery, given in Egypt on the night before the exodus, was a prophecy waiting fifteen centuries for its fulfilment. That is how the ceremonial law should be read throughout — not as arbitrary ritual to be excused, and not as a code to be reimposed, but as a shadow whose every edge was cast by a body that was coming.
roots_summary: Hebrew bashal (H1310), to boil, to seethe, to ripen; tsalah (H6748), to roast; bashel, boiled — the contrast of Exodus 12:9.
roots_lines: Hebrew bashal (H1310) — to boil, seethe, or cook; also to ripen, of grapes; Exodus 12:9, Leviticus 6:28, Numbers 6:19.
Hebrew tsalah (H6748) — to roast over fire; the required method for the passover lamb; Exodus 12:8-9, Isaiah 44:16.
Hebrew na' (H4995) — raw, underdone; the first thing forbidden in the passover rule; Exodus 12:9.
usage: “Nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire” — the lamb kept whole and put through the fire.
“The earthen vessel wherein it is sodden shall be broken” — what has touched the holy thing does not return to common use.
“He will not have sodden flesh of thee, but raw” — the sons of Eli refusing to let God's portion go up first.

pos: v. (to strip off the skin; in the law, the priestly act of skinning the burnt offering)
etymology: Old English flean, to strip off skin. A butcher's word, used by Moses of the altar and by Micah of tyrants.
biblical_def: The burnt offering came apart under the priest's hand in a fixed order: “And he shall flay the burnt offering, and cut it into his pieces” (Lev 1:6). Nothing was hidden. The skin came off, and everything the hide had covered was exposed, washed, and laid on the fire — the inwards and the legs washed in water, the whole burnt as a sweet savour unto the LORD. That is the meaning of the whole burnt offering: not a portion given and the rest retained, but the entire animal opened up and consumed. Hezekiah's revival ran into the practical cost of it: “the priests were too few, so that they could not flay all the burnt offerings” (2Ch 29:34), and the Levites, more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests, did the work until it was ended — a rebuke recorded in Scripture against a professional ministry outpaced in zeal by its helpers. Micah takes the same verb and turns it on the rulers of Israel who “eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them” (Mic 3:3). The priest flays the sacrifice; the tyrant flays the people. Both images are in the book, and the prophets never let the second hide behind the first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to flay as to skin; to strip off the skin of an animal; to take off the skin or surface.
webster_full: FLAY, v.t. To skin; to strip off the skin of an animal.
2. To take off the skin or surface of any thing; as, to flay the ground.
FLAYED, pp. Skinned; stripped of the skin.
scriptures: Lev 1:6
And he shall flay the burnt offering, and cut it into his pieces.
Mic 3:3
Who also eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them; and they break their bones, and chop them in pieces, as for the pot, and as flesh within the caldron.
Rom 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
corruption_summary: Micah 3 names the sin of shepherds who feed on the flock, and it has an exact modern form in ministries built to extract from the people they were given to feed.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah 3:1-3 is one of the fiercest passages in the prophets, and it is aimed not at pagans but at the heads of Jacob and the princes of the house of Israel: who hate the good, and love the evil; who pluck off their skin from off them, and their flesh from off their bones; who eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them. The figure is deliberately unbearable. The men appointed to guard the flock are pictured butchering it and boiling it in a pot. Ezekiel 34 makes the same charge in the language of shepherds who feed themselves and not the sheep, and it is the passage against which the Lord sets Himself as the good shepherd who gives His life for them. The corruption is perennial and it is not confined to any one tradition: the ministry treated as a living to be extracted rather than a stewardship to be given, the flock valued by what can be got from it. Peter states the standard for elders exactly against this: feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind (1Pe 5:2). And the pattern for every Christian is Romans 12:1 — the burnt offering flayed and wholly given, applied now to a living body presented to God.
roots_summary: Hebrew pashat (H6584), to strip off, to flay, also to make a raid; 'olah (H5930), the burnt offering, literally that which goes up; Hebrew 'or (H5785), skin.
roots_lines: Hebrew pashat (H6584) — to strip, to flay, to invade; used of the priest with the offering and of the tyrant with the people; Leviticus 1:6, Micah 3:3.
Hebrew 'olah (H5930) — the burnt offering, that which ascends; the whole animal consumed, none retained; Leviticus 1:3-9.
Hebrew 'or (H5785) — skin, hide; the skin of the burnt offering became the officiating priest's portion; Leviticus 7:8.
usage: “He shall flay the burnt offering, and cut it into his pieces” — nothing covered, nothing withheld.
“The priests were too few, so that they could not flay all the burnt offerings” — Hezekiah's revival outrunning the ministry.
“Flay their skin from off them” — Micah on rulers who feed upon the flock.

pos: n. (the fat tail of the eastern sheep, taken off hard by the backbone and burnt on the altar)
etymology: Middle English rumpe, of Scandinavian origin, the hind part. The Hebrew 'alyah names the heavy fat tail of the broad-tailed sheep of the Near East, a prized portion.
biblical_def: In the peace offering the rump is named with precision: “the fat thereof, and the whole rump, it shall he take off hard by the backbone” (Lev 3:9), and it goes on the altar with the fat that covers the inwards, the two kidneys, and the caul above the liver. The same portion belongs to the ram of consecration (Exo 29:22), to Aaron's ordination (Lev 8:25), and to the offerings of the eighth day (Lev 9:19). The broad-tailed sheep of Syria and Palestine carries a tail of solid fat that may weigh many pounds, and it was the choicest eating in the flock. That is exactly why the law claims it. The standing rule of Leviticus is that all the fat is the LORD's (Lev 3:16), and Israel was forbidden to eat it. God does not take the offal; He takes the best cut, the richest part, the piece a man would have chosen for himself — and He takes it first, before any of the peace offering is eaten in fellowship. Abel brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof, and the LORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the rump as the end of the backbone of an animal, with the parts adjacent; the buttocks; and among certain eastern sheep, the fat tail.
webster_full: RUMP, n. The end of the back bone of an animal with the parts adjacent.
2. The buttocks.
In the Levitical law, the fat tail of the sheep, appointed to be burnt upon the altar with the fat of the inwards.
scriptures: Lev 3:9

And he shall offer of the sacrifice of the peace offering an offering made by fire unto the LORD; the fat thereof, and the whole rump, it shall he take off hard by the backbone; and the fat that covereth the inwards, and all the fat that is upon the inwards,

Also thou shalt take of the ram the fat and the rump, and the fat that covereth the inwards, and the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys, and the fat that is upon them, and the right shoulder; for it is a ram of consecration:
Lev 3:16
And the priest shall burn them upon the altar: it is the food of the offering made by fire for a sweet savour: all the fat is the LORD's.
corruption_summary: Giving God the leftover — the spare hour, the residual income, the attention that remains after everything else has been served — is the exact inversion of a law that claimed the fat tail first.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The rump is a cut of meat and nobody is redefining it. The principle to recover is the one Leviticus states flatly: all the fat is the LORD's. In a flock of broad-tailed sheep the fat tail was the delicacy, and God claimed it by statute, together with the kidneys and the caul, and forbade Israel to eat it. He did not ask for what was left over after the family had eaten; He asked for the piece the family most wanted. Malachi 1 shows what happens when that order is quietly reversed: the priests brought the blind, the lame, and the sick for sacrifice, and the LORD's answer was, Offer it now unto thy governor; will he be pleased with thee? The modern form is rarely a defective animal. It is a calendar and a budget in which God receives the remainder — the hour when nothing else needs doing, the giving that is possible after every other obligation is met, the attention left at the end of a spent day. Firstfruits, firstborn, and the fat tail are one doctrine: what is given to God is given first and it is the best, or it is not really given at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'alyah (H451), the fat tail of the eastern sheep; cheleb (H2459), fat, the best or choicest part; 'atsel, hard by, close beside — the backbone of Leviticus 3:9.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'alyah (H451) — the fat tail of the broad-tailed sheep; named in every list of the altar portions; Exodus 29:22, Leviticus 3:9, 8:25, 9:19.
Hebrew cheleb (H2459) — fat, and by extension the choicest part of anything; the fat of the land, the finest of the wheat; Leviticus 3:16, Genesis 45:18.
Hebrew kilyah (H3629) — the kidneys, the reins; burnt with the fat, and used figuratively for the innermost affections God tries; Leviticus 3:4, Psalm 26:2.
usage: “The whole rump…take off hard by the backbone” — the choicest cut claimed by statute.
“The fat and the rump…for it is a ram of consecration” — the ordination of Aaron and his sons.
“All the fat is the LORD's” — the standing rule behind every list.

pos: adj. (having something in excess; in the law, a beast or a man with a member overgrown or malformed, disqualified from the altar or the priesthood)
etymology: Latin superfluus, overflowing, from super, above, and fluere, to flow. In Leviticus the word covers any part in excess, as lacking covers any part deficient.
biblical_def: The law of the priesthood lists the disqualifying blemishes and includes “a blind man, or a lame, or he that hath a flat nose, or any thing superfluous” (Lev 21:18). The law of the offerings applies the same standard to the animal: a bullock or lamb “that hath any thing superfluous or lacking in his parts” may be offered for a freewill offering, “but for a vow it shall not be accepted” (Lev 22:23). Two things must be said carefully. First, this is not a judgment on the worth of the disabled man. The blemished priest was not cast out of Israel and not cut off from the sanctuary's benefits — the very next verse provides that he shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy (Lev 21:22). He was barred from officiating, not from belonging. Second, the whole standard exists to say something about the Priest who was coming: holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, without blemish and without spot. Paul then uses the same adjective in an entirely ordinary sense: “as touching the ministering to the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you” (2Co 9:1) — unnecessary, because their willingness was already known.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines superfluous as more than is wanted; unnecessary; useless; and, of a part, exceeding what is natural or requisite.
webster_full: SUPERFLUOUS, a. More than is wanted, or is sufficient; rendering more than enough; unnecessary; useless.
2. Unnecessary; not required by the circumstances of the case.
In Scripture, of a member exceeding what is natural, and so disqualifying for the priesthood or the altar.
scriptures: For whatsoever man he be that hath a blemish, he shall not approach: a blind man, or a lame, or he that hath a flat nose, or any thing superfluous,
Either a bullock or a lamb that hath any thing superfluous or lacking in his parts, that mayest thou offer for a freewill offering; but for a vow it shall not be accepted.
But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:
corruption_summary: The blemish laws are read either as ancient cruelty toward the disabled or as a warrant for judging people by their bodies, and Leviticus 21:22 refutes both in a single verse.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 21 is regularly produced as evidence that the God of the Old Testament despised the disabled, and the charge is answered inside the chapter itself. The blemished son of Aaron did not lose his priestly standing, his inheritance, his family, or his access to God. Verse 22 is explicit: he shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy. He was excluded from one thing only — the act of officiating at the altar — and he was excluded for the same reason a lamb with anything superfluous or lacking was excluded from a vow offering: because everything at that altar was a picture, and the picture had to be exact. The whole apparatus was pointing at one unblemished Priest offering one unblemished Lamb, and a marred symbol would have preached a marred gospel. The opposite abuse is worse and appears within the church: the use of these chapters as a general licence to weigh people by their bodies, their appearance, or their capacities. James 2 forbids it outright, the Lord chose the weak things and the base things and the things that are despised, and 2 Corinthians 12 puts the apostolic ministry itself in a body with a thorn. Israel's altar required perfection because Christ was coming; the church requires faith because He has come.
roots_summary: Hebrew sarua' (H8311), stretched out, deformed by excess; qalat (H7038), stunted, lacking; mum (H3971), a blemish; Greek perissos (G4053), abundant, superfluous.
roots_lines: Hebrew sarua' (H8311) — extended, overgrown, having a member in excess; Leviticus 21:18, 22:23.
Hebrew mum (H3971) — a blemish, a spot; the disqualifying mark on priest or victim, and denied of the Servant; Leviticus 21:17-21, Daniel 1:4.
Greek perissos (G4053) — over and above, more than enough; Paul's ordinary use in the collection chapters; 2 Corinthians 9:1.
usage: “Or any thing superfluous” — the blemish list for the priesthood.
“Superfluous or lacking in his parts” — excess and deficiency alike disqualify a vow offering.
“It is superfluous for me to write to you” — Paul's ordinary sense: unnecessary.

pos: n. (the liquor in which flesh has been boiled)
etymology: Old English broth, from the same root as brew. In the Authorized Version it appears at two opposite tables: Gideon's offering under the oak, and the idolaters' vessels of Isaiah 65.
biblical_def: Gideon, having been told he should save Israel and asking for a sign, went in and made ready a kid and unleavened cakes, put the flesh in a basket and the broth in a pot, and brought it out to the angel under the oak (Jdg 6:19). The instruction he received turned the meal into a sacrifice: “Take the flesh and the unleavened cakes, and lay them upon this rock, and pour out the broth” (Jdg 6:20). What Gideon had prepared as hospitality was poured out on a rock, and fire rose out of the rock and consumed it. He had meant to feed a guest; he was taught to worship. Isaiah shows the other table: a rebellious people “which remain among the graves, and lodge in the monuments, which eat swine's flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels” (Isa 65:4) — necromancy and forbidden meat together, with the pot as the evidence. The Authorized Version thus uses this small domestic word to mark two possibilities for anything a man prepares: it may be poured out on the rock and consumed by God's own fire, or it may sit in his vessels as an abomination.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines broth as liquor in which flesh has been boiled and its substance extracted; a decoction of flesh, usually with vegetables.
webster_full: BROTH, n. Liquor in which flesh has been boiled and its substance extracted.
2. A decoction of flesh, usually with rice or other ingredients.
Take the flesh and the unleavened cakes, and lay them upon this rock, and pour out the broth. Judges vi.
scriptures: Jdg 6:20
And the angel of God said unto him, Take the flesh and the unleavened cakes, and lay them upon this rock, and pour out the broth. And he did so.
Isa 65:4
Which remain among the graves, and lodge in the monuments, which eat swine's flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;
Jdg 6:21

Then the angel of the LORD put forth the end of the staff that was in his hand, and touched the flesh and the unleavened cakes; and there rose up fire out of the rock, and consumed the flesh and the unleavened cakes. Then the angel of the LORD departed out of his sight.
corruption_summary: Gideon's meal is often preached as a lesson in hospitality or in seeking signs, and the actual turn of the scene — a supper commanded to be poured out as a sacrifice — is passed over.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Broth is broth. But the scene under the oak at Ophrah deserves better handling than it usually gets. Gideon prepared a costly meal — a whole kid and an ephah of flour in a season when Midian had left Israel nothing — and he brought it out as food for a guest. The angel would not eat it. Lay it on this rock, and pour out the broth: that is, this is not a dinner, it is an offering, and the rock is an altar. Fire rose out of the rock and took it, and Gideon, who had begun the conversation arguing that the LORD had forsaken them, built an altar there and called it Jehovahshalom. The principle to recover is that God frequently accepts what we bring by transforming what it is for. A man offers his work, his house, his money, his gift, as hospitality toward God — something done for Him on his own terms — and finds it commanded onto the rock instead, poured out, consumed, and answered with fire. Isaiah 65:4 is the alternative in the same idiom: a pot kept in one's own vessels, full of what God forbade.
roots_summary: Hebrew maraq (H4839), broth, the liquor of boiled flesh; paraq, to pour out; bashal (H1310), to boil or seethe.
roots_lines: Hebrew maraq (H4839) — broth, soup, the liquor of boiled flesh; used only of Gideon's pot and of the idolaters' vessels; Judges 6:19-20, Isaiah 65:4.
Hebrew bashal (H1310) — to boil, to seethe; the cooking that produces the broth; Judges 6:19, Exodus 12:9.
Hebrew tsuwr (H6697) — a rock; the rock at Ophrah that became an altar and gave up fire; Judges 6:20-21, Deuteronomy 32:4.
usage: “Lay them upon this rock, and pour out the broth” — a supper turned into a sacrifice.
“There rose up fire out of the rock” — the answer to what was poured out.
“Broth of abominable things is in their vessels” — the other table, kept in a man's own pot.

pos: n. (the mother of a beast or bird; the female parent among animals)
etymology: A variant of dame, from Latin domina, mistress. In the Authorized Version it is never a barrier of water; it is always a mother.
biblical_def: Three laws use the word and they belong together. The firstborn of oxen and sheep is claimed for God, but not immediately: “seven days it shall be with his dam; on the eighth day thou shalt give it me” (Exo 22:30); and again, “it shall be seven days under the dam; and from the eighth day and thenceforth it shall be accepted for an offering made by fire unto the LORD” (Lev 22:27). Even in claiming His own, God will not have the newborn torn from its mother on the first day. Then the law of the nest: “If a bird's nest chance to be before thee in the way…and the dam sitting upon the young, or upon the eggs, thou shalt not take the dam with the young: But thou shalt in any wise let the dam go, and take the young to thee” (Deu 22:6-7). A man may take the eggs; he may not take the mother with them, because that ends the line. And to this smallest of commandments is attached one of the great promises: that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days — the same promise as the fifth commandment, hung on a bird's nest. The God who numbers the sparrows legislates for them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dam as a female parent, used of beasts, particularly of quadrupeds; the mother of an animal.
webster_full: DAM, n. A female parent; used of beasts, particularly of quadrupeds.
DAM, n. A mole, bank or mound of earth, or any wall or frame of wood, intended to confine water.
Thou shalt not take the dam with the young. Deut. xxii.
scriptures: Likewise shalt thou do with thine oxen, and with thy sheep: seven days it shall be with his dam; on the eighth day thou shalt give it me.
Deu 22:6

If a bird's nest chance to be before thee in the way in any tree, or on the ground, whether they be young ones, or eggs, and the dam sitting upon the young, or upon the eggs, thou shalt not take the dam with the young:
Deu 22:7
But thou shalt in any wise let the dam go, and take the young to thee; that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days.
corruption_summary: The law of the nest is claimed by two camps — the one that makes animals bearers of rights equal to man, and the one that treats the creation as raw material — and Deuteronomy 22 refutes both by making it a matter of dominion under law.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 22:6-7 is a small law with a large promise, and it is regularly pressed into service by two opposite errors. The first reads it as an early charter of animal rights and concludes that the creature stands on the same footing as the man. The text does not say so: the man may take the young; the beast is given for his use; and the whole passage assumes the dominion of Genesis 1:28. The second error is the reverse and is far more common in practice: the treatment of the creation as inert raw material, whose only value is what can be extracted from it this quarter. That is the reading the law forbids. A man may take the eggs, but not in a way that ends the nest; the mother goes free, and the future of the species with her. Proverbs 12:10 states the principle: a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast. This is stewardship, not sentiment, and the two are distinguished by whose the earth is — the earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof, so a man handles what is not his own and answers for it. The promise attached is startling: it may be well with thee, and thou mayest prolong thy days. God fastened long life to how a man behaves toward a bird when nobody is watching.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'em (H517), mother, dam; qen (H7064), a nest; shalach (H7971), to let go, to send away — the command concerning the mother bird.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'em (H517) — mother; the ordinary word for a human mother, used of the beast and the bird in these laws; Exodus 22:30, Deuteronomy 22:6.
Hebrew qen (H7064) — a nest; the same noun used of Noah's rooms in the ark and of the eagle stirring up her nest; Deuteronomy 22:6, Deuteronomy 32:11.
Hebrew shalach (H7971) — to send away, to let go; the mother bird released, the same verb as Let my people go; Deuteronomy 22:7, Exodus 5:1.
usage: “Seven days it shall be with his dam” — even what God claims is not torn away on the first day.
“Thou shalt not take the dam with the young” — the eggs may be taken; the future may not.
“That it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days” — a great promise on a small law.

pos: adj. (having four feet; quadruped; used of the beasts in Peter's vision and in Paul's indictment of idolatry)
etymology: A plain English compound rendering the Greek tetrapous, four-footed. It appears only three times in the Authorized Version and every occurrence is theologically loaded.
biblical_def: Twice the word describes the sheet let down from heaven at Joppa: “Wherein were all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air” (Act 10:12), and Peter repeats the inventory when he rehearses the vision to the church at Jerusalem (Act 11:6). Three times the voice said Rise, Peter; kill, and eat; three times he refused; three times the answer came, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. The vision was not finally about food. Peter says so himself when he walks into Cornelius' house: God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean. The third occurrence turns the same catalogue into an indictment: men “changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things” (Rom 1:23). Paul is running down the ladder of creation deliberately — man, then birds, then quadrupeds, then reptiles — describing worship in freefall. The same list that comes down from heaven at Joppa as a declaration of cleansing goes up from the heathen altar as the substance of idolatry, and the difference is entirely in the direction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fourfooted as having four feet; quadruped.
webster_full: FOUR-FOOTED, a. Having four feet; quadruped; as a four-footed beast.
QUADRUPED, n. An animal having four legs or feet, as a horse, an ox or a lion.
In Scripture, the four-footed beasts are named with the fowls and creeping things in the sheet let down to Peter.
scriptures: Wherein were all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.
Act 11:6
Upon the which when I had fastened mine eyes, I considered, and saw fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.
Rom 1:23
And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.
corruption_summary: Peter's sheet is quoted to prove that God accepts everything He once called unclean, which stands the vision on its head: it declared the Gentiles cleansed by Christ's blood, not sin re-labelled.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 10:15 — what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common — has become one of the most misused sentences in the New Testament. It is now regularly produced to argue that conduct Scripture names as sin has been declared acceptable, and that anyone who still calls it sin is playing Peter's part in the story. The vision says the opposite of that. Its subject is not conduct but persons, and Peter tells us so twice: God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean (Act 10:28), and, God, which knoweth the hearts, bare them witness…purifying their hearts by faith (Act 15:8-9). The Gentiles were cleansed — not declared to have needed no cleansing. The cleansing agent is named in the same chapter: whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins. And the very household that received the sheet's meaning received also the apostolic preaching of repentance. To use the vision as a warrant for calling sin clean is to take a text about the blood of Christ washing unclean people and turn it into a text about there being no uncleanness to wash. Romans 1:23, with the same list of creatures, is a reminder of where a religion goes once it starts revising what God has said.
roots_summary: Greek tetrapous (G5074), four-footed; koinos (G2839), common, unclean; katharizo (G2511), to cleanse — the verb of Acts 10:15.
roots_lines: Greek tetrapous (G5074) — four-footed, a quadruped; used only of the sheet at Joppa and of the idols of Romans 1; Acts 10:12, 11:6, Romans 1:23.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, and so ceremonially unclean; Peter's protest, and his corrected verdict on men; Acts 10:14, 10:28.
Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse, to purify; what God has done, and the ground on which nothing He cleansed may be called common; Acts 10:15, 15:9, 1 John 1:7.
usage: “All manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth” — the sheet let down three times at Joppa.
“I considered, and saw fourfooted beasts” — Peter rehearsing the vision to Jerusalem.
“Changed the glory of the uncorruptible God…to…fourfooted beasts” — worship in freefall.

pos: n. pl. (dead bodies; the slain)
etymology: Latin corpus, a body, through Old French cors. The Authorized Version uses it of two battlefields: the Assyrian camp before Jerusalem, and Nineveh under judgment.
biblical_def: The word marks the morning after the greatest deliverance in Judah's history. Sennacherib had blasphemed the living God by the mouth of Rabshakeh, Hezekiah spread the letter before the LORD in the house, and Isaiah sent word that the king of Assyria should not come into this city nor shoot an arrow there. “And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the LORD went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses” (2Ki 19:35); Isaiah records the same in his own book (Isa 37:36). Not a Judean soldier drew a sword. The blasphemy was answered by one angel in one night, and Sennacherib went home to be murdered by his sons in the house of his god. Nahum then uses the word of Nineveh's own end: “there is a multitude of slain, and a great number of carcases; and there is none end of their corpses; they stumble upon their corpses” (Nah 3:3). The city spared under Jonah's preaching, a century repented and then relapsed, received at last the judgment it had escaped. God is longsuffering and He is not mocked, and both facts stand in the same book.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a corpse as the dead body of a human being; a carcase.
webster_full: CORPSE, n. The dead body of a human being.
2. A carcase; the remains of the dead.
They arose early in the morning, and behold, they were all dead corpses. 2 Kings xix.
scriptures: And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the LORD went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.
Then the angel of the LORD went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand: and when they arose early in the morning, behold, they were all dead corpses.
Nah 3:3

The horseman lifteth up both the bright sword and the glittering spear: and there is a multitude of slain, and a great number of carcases; and there is none end of their corpses; they stumble upon their corpses:
corruption_summary: The deliverance at Jerusalem is regularly rewritten as a plague or a legend, on the assumption that a report of direct divine judgment cannot be historical — which is a philosophical commitment, not a finding.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern handling of 2 Kings 19:35 is to look for a natural mechanism — a plague in the camp, mice gnawing bowstrings after Herodotus, a political recall to Nineveh — and to treat the angel of the LORD as the way an ancient writer reported an epidemic. The dictionary declines the framework, because it is not a conclusion drawn from evidence but an assumption brought to it: that God does not act directly in history, and therefore that any text reporting such an act must be reporting something else. Scripture presents the event as the answer to a specific prayer over a specific letter, foretold by a named prophet, in a specific year, against a king whose own annals confirm that he besieged Jerusalem and, alone among his campaigns, never claimed to have taken it. Isaiah 37 is not a legend appended centuries later; it is the vindication of the LORD's own words, Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? even against the Holy One of Israel. The dictionary holds the canonical narrative as the authoritative account, with archaeology and the Assyrian records as corroborative rather than as the court of appeal. And Nahum keeps the balance: the same God who spared Nineveh at Jonah's preaching brought it to an end when its repentance failed.
roots_summary: Hebrew peger (H6297), a carcase, a corpse; chalal (H2491), the slain, one pierced through; mal'ak YHWH, the angel of the LORD.
roots_lines: Hebrew peger (H6297) — a carcase, a dead body; the Assyrian camp at dawn and the fallen carcases in the wilderness; 2 Kings 19:35, Numbers 14:29.
Hebrew chalal (H2491) — the slain, one pierced or fatally wounded; Nahum's multitude in the streets of Nineveh; Nahum 3:3, Isaiah 53:5 uses the cognate verb of the Servant.
Hebrew mal'ak (H4397) — a messenger, an angel; one angel sufficed for the whole camp; 2 Kings 19:35, Psalm 34:7.
usage: “Behold, they were all dead corpses” — the morning after the answer to Hezekiah's prayer.
“The angel of the LORD went forth” — Isaiah's record of the same night.
“They stumble upon their corpses” — Nineveh at last.

pos: adj. (devouring with rapacity; furiously voracious; used of beasts and of birds of prey)
etymology: Old French ravine, plunder, from Latin rapina, robbery. To be ravenous is to be given to seizing and tearing.
biblical_def: The word marks three very different things. In the highway of holiness it marks an absence: “No lion shall be there, nor any ravenous beast shall go up thereon, it shall not be found there; but the redeemed shall walk there” (Isa 35:9). The safety of that road is defined by what cannot get onto it. In Isaiah 46:11 it marks an instrument: God calls “a ravenous bird from the east, the man that executeth my counsel from a far country” — Cyrus, a pagan king, named a bird of prey and employed by name, and the verse closes with the great declaration, I have spoken it, I will also bring it to pass; I have purposed it, I will also do it. That is the doctrine of providence in its strongest form: God governs the raptor. And in Ezekiel 39:4 it marks a judgment, Gog given to the ravenous birds of every sort. The Lord Jesus then takes the same image into the church: beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. The ravenous thing is never at home among the redeemed; when it appears there, it appears in a disguise, and Christ tells us to know it by its fruits.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ravenous as furiously voracious; hungry even to rage; devouring with rapacious eagerness; and, of a bird or beast, given to prey.
webster_full: RAVENOUS, a. Furiously voracious; hungry even to rage; devouring with rapacious eagerness; as a ravenous lion or wolf.
2. Eager for prey or gratification; as a ravenous appetite.
RAVEN, v.t. To devour with great eagerness; to eat with voracity.
scriptures: Isa 35:9
No lion shall be there, nor any ravenous beast shall go up thereon, it shall not be found there; but the redeemed shall walk there:
Calling a ravenous bird from the east, the man that executeth my counsel from a far country: yea, I have spoken it, I will also bring it to pass; I have purposed it, I will also do it.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
corruption_summary: The Lord's warning about wolves in sheep's clothing is applied confidently to teachers in other camps and almost never to the pulpit one already trusts, which is precisely the blindness the warning was given to prevent.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 7:15 is quoted constantly and applied almost exclusively outward. That is a problem, because the clothing is the whole point of the warning. A wolf that looked like a wolf would need no warning; the danger described is a teacher who presents every visible mark of a sheep and is inwardly ravening. This means the detection cannot be by appearance, by manner, by success, or by orthodoxy of vocabulary, and the Lord gives the only test that works: ye shall know them by their fruits — over time, in the life, in what is left behind. Peter's second epistle and Jude fill in the picture with unsettling specificity: covetousness, feigned words, making merchandise of the flock, promising liberty while being themselves the servants of corruption. Every one of those can coexist for years with sound doctrinal statements and full auditoriums. The corruption is not that people fail to believe in wolves; it is that everyone is confident the wolves are in the other camp. Isaiah 46:11 supplies the comfort that keeps this from becoming paranoia: God calls the ravenous bird Himself, and rules it, and His counsel shall stand.
roots_summary: Hebrew pariyts (H6530), violent, a robber; 'ayit (H5861), a bird of prey; Greek harpax (G727), rapacious, ravening, an extortioner.
roots_lines: Hebrew pariyts (H6530) — violent, a breaker-in, a robber; the ravenous beast barred from the highway of holiness, and the den of robbers in Jeremiah 7:11; Isaiah 35:9.
Hebrew 'ayit (H5861) — a bird of prey, a screamer; the fowls that came down on Abram's carcases, and Cyrus called from the east; Genesis 15:11, Isaiah 46:11.
Greek harpax (G727) — rapacious, ravening; used of the wolves in sheep's clothing and of the extortioner in Paul's vice lists; Matthew 7:15, 1 Corinthians 5:11.
usage: “Nor any ravenous beast shall go up thereon” — the highway of holiness defined by what cannot enter it.
“Calling a ravenous bird from the east” — God governing the raptor for His own counsel.
“Inwardly they are ravening wolves” — the disguise, and the test of fruits.

pos: n. pl. (venomous serpents; used in Scripture chiefly as a figure of deadly speech)
etymology: Greek aspis, through Latin, a small venomous snake of Egypt and Libya. The Hebrew pethen is a cobra or adder whose poison is proverbial.
biblical_def: Moses' song sets the standard image: the wine of the enemy nations “is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps” (Deu 32:33) — what men drink down as pleasure is in fact venom. Zophar, in Job, applies it to swallowed wickedness: “his meat in his bowels is turned, it is the gall of asps within him” (Job 20:14), and “he shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him” (Job 20:16). Sin is sweet in the mouth and turns in the belly. Then Paul, assembling the indictment of the whole human race from the Psalms and Isaiah, brings the image to its resting place: “Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Rom 3:13). That is quoted from Psalm 140:3, and its position in Romans 3 is deliberate: Paul has been proving that there is none righteous, no, not one, and the largest single portion of his evidence concerns the mouth — throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, eyes, in that order. The tongue is the organ by which total depravity is most easily demonstrated, and Scripture puts a cobra under it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the asp as a small venomous serpent of Egypt and Libya, whose bite is fatal and, it was anciently said, occasions little pain.
webster_full: ASP, ASPIC, n. A small venomous serpent of Egypt and Libya, whose bite occasions inevitable death.
The bite of the asp is said to occasion little pain, and the person dies as if in a slumber.
The poison of asps is under their lips. Rom. iii.
scriptures: Their wine is the poison of dragons, and the cruel venom of asps.
He shall suck the poison of asps: the viper's tongue shall slay him.
Rom 3:13
Their throat is an open sepulchre; with their tongues they have used deceit; the poison of asps is under their lips:
corruption_summary: Romans 3's catalogue is read as hyperbole about especially wicked people, when Paul's whole argument requires that it be the true description of every man by nature, including the religious one reading it.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 3:10-18 is a chain of Old Testament quotations, and Paul assembles it for a stated purpose: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God (Rom 3:19). The catalogue is therefore not a description of criminals; it is the verdict on the race, and Paul has spent two chapters closing every exit — the pagan in chapter 1, the moralist at the start of chapter 2, the Jew with the law in the rest of it — specifically so that the reader cannot place himself outside the indictment. The common softening reads these verses as vivid overstatement about particularly bad men, which quietly converts the passage from a doctrine of total depravity into a piece of rhetoric about other people. The Reformed confessions take Paul at his word. Total depravity does not mean that every man is as wicked as he could be; it means that no part of him — mind, will, affections, tongue — is undamaged, and that nothing in him inclines him to God. The poison of asps under the lips is a strong figure, and it is aimed at the reader. Only a man who has heard it aimed at himself has any use for the verse that follows the indictment: being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
roots_summary: Hebrew pethen (H6620), an asp, a cobra; chemah (H2534), venom, heat, fury; Greek aspis (G785), an asp.
roots_lines: Hebrew pethen (H6620) — an asp or cobra; the deaf adder that will not hear the charmer, and the serpent the weaned child shall play beside in the peaceable kingdom; Psalm 58:4, Isaiah 11:8.
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, poison, fury; the cruel venom of asps in the song of Moses; Deuteronomy 32:33, Psalm 58:4.
Greek aspis (G785) — an asp; used once, in Paul's indictment of the tongue; Romans 3:13.
usage: “The cruel venom of asps” — what men drink as pleasure.
“He shall suck the poison of asps” — sin sweet in the mouth and turned in the belly.
“The poison of asps is under their lips” — the indictment of the race, aimed at the reader.

pos: n. pl. (small rodents; unclean under the law, and the figures cast in gold by the Philistines as a trespass offering)
etymology: Old English mys, plural of mus. The Hebrew 'akbar covers mice and rats generally; they are listed among the creeping things that are unclean.
biblical_def: The strangest offering in Scripture was made by pagans. The Philistines had taken the ark, and it had ruined them city by city — Dagon fallen and broken on his own threshold, the people smitten with emerods, the land marred by mice. Their priests and diviners advised them to send it home with a trespass offering: “Five golden emerods, and five golden mice, according to the number of the lords of the Philistines: for one plague was on you all, and on your lords” (1Sa 6:4). They were to make “images of your mice that mar the land; and ye shall give glory unto the God of Israel” (1Sa 6:5). So the coffer went beside the ark with the mice of gold in it (1Sa 6:11), and the golden mice were counted according to the number of all the cities (1Sa 6:18). Two lessons stand out. First, the heathen knew the hand that was on them and confessed it in gold. Second, they still handled the holy thing on their own terms — a new cart, kine that had never been yoked — and Israel afterward copied the cart, and Uzzah died. The ark judged those who took it and those who received it back, and God is not casual about His own holiness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives mice as the plural of mouse, a small animal of the genus Mus, infesting houses and fields.
webster_full: MICE, n. plu. of mouse.
MOUSE, n. A small animal of the genus Mus, inhabiting houses. The name is also applied to many other species of the genus.
In Scripture, an unclean creeping thing, and the figure cast in gold by the Philistines with the emerods.
scriptures: And they laid the ark of the LORD upon the cart, and the coffer with the mice of gold and the images of their emerods.
These also shall be unclean unto you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth; the weasel, and the mouse, and the tortoise after his kind,
They that sanctify themselves, and purify themselves in the gardens behind one tree in the midst, eating swine's flesh, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The Philistines' golden mice are an unimprovable picture of a religion that acknowledges God's power, pays Him tribute, and still will not come to Him on His own terms.
corruption_paragraphs: The men of Ashdod, Gath and Ekron were not atheists. They had felt the hand of the God of Israel on their bodies and their fields for seven months, they said so publicly, and they paid in gold. Their diviners even preached a sermon out of Israel's history: wherefore then do ye harden your hearts, as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? What they would not do was submit. They sent the ark away rather than seek the God who owned it; they sent Him tribute rather than themselves. That arrangement has never gone out of fashion. It appears wherever God is acknowledged as real and powerful, credited with the blessings and blamed for the losses, offered money, ceremony, and public respect — and never obeyed. James calls the intellectual half of this the faith of devils, who believe and tremble. Isaiah 66:17 names the other half: people who sanctify and purify themselves in the gardens while eating the mouse and the swine, religion and abomination kept in the same house.
