The mercy of 1 Samuel 6 is that God took His own ark home; the warning of 1 Samuel 6:19 and of Uzzah is that He will be sanctified in them that come nigh Him, whether Philistine or Israelite.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'akbar (H5909), a mouse or field-rat; 'asham (H817), a trespass or guilt offering; sherets (H8318), a swarming or creeping thing.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'akbar (H5909) — a mouse, a field-rat; unclean in Leviticus, cast in gold by the Philistines, and eaten in the forbidden gardens of Isaiah 66; Leviticus 11:29, 1 Samuel 6:4, Isaiah 66:17.
Hebrew 'asham (H817) — a trespass offering, guilt and the payment for it; what the Philistines sent with the ark; 1 Samuel 6:3-4, Leviticus 5:15.
Hebrew sherets (H8318) — a swarming or creeping thing; the class of unclean creatures to which the mouse belongs; Leviticus 11:29-31.
usage: “Five golden emerods, and five golden mice” — the trespass offering of the Philistine lords.
“Images of your mice that mar the land” — a confession cast in gold.
“The abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together” — religion and abomination kept in one house.

pos: n. (a broad open vessel for food; the platter from which a meal is eaten in common)
etymology: Old English disc, from Latin discus, a quoit or disc, hence a flat plate. The word carries the whole weight of table fellowship in the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Jael brought Sisera “butter in a lordly dish” (Jdg 5:25) — he asked water and got milk, served in the best vessel in the tent, and the honour of that dish is what makes the hammer and the nail so terrible a few lines later. Isaiah's image of Jerusalem's desolation is domestic and merciless: “I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down” (2Ki 21:13). But the word's greatest moment is the upper room. “He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me” (Mat 26:23); Mark has it, “It is one of the twelve, that dippeth with me in the dish” (Mar 14:20). In the ancient East, to eat from one dish was the strongest bond of loyalty a man could enter; the sop given to Judas was, by the custom of that table, a mark of particular favour from the host. The Lord names the betrayer by the very act of sharing food with him, quoting the psalm as He does it: he that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me. The dish is a small round vessel, and it holds the whole doctrine of treachery.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dish as a broad open vessel, made of various materials, in which provisions are served at table; also the meat or provisions served in a dish.
webster_full: DISH, n. A broad open vessel, made of various materials, in which provisions are served at table.
2. The meat or provisions served in a dish; hence, any particular kind of food.
DISH, v.t. To put in a dish; to serve in a dish or dishes for the table.
scriptures: Jdg 5:25
He asked water, and she gave him milk; she brought forth butter in a lordly dish.
And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down.
And he answered and said, He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me.
corruption_summary: Judas is repeatedly rehabilitated — as the misunderstood zealot, the necessary instrument, even the truest disciple — and the shared dish is the detail that makes every such reading impossible.
corruption_paragraphs: A steady stream of popular treatments recasts Judas as a man forcing the Messiah's hand, or as a scapegoat, or, in the Gnostic Gospel of Judas revived with much publicity in 2006, as the one disciple who understood and obeyed a secret instruction. Every one of these readings has to get past the dish. The Lord did not identify His betrayer at a distance; He identified him by the intimacy of a shared bowl and a handed sop, which in that culture was the host's particular kindness, and He quoted Psalm 41:9 while doing it: mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me. Scripture is emphatic on both halves of the mystery and softens neither: the Son of man goeth as it is written of him — the betrayal was foreordained and prophesied — but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! Divine decree and human guilt stand together in one verse, which is the confessional position exactly: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, and is not the author of sin, and the creature's will is not violated. Judas was not an instrument acquitted by prophecy. He was a thief who kept the bag, who took thirty pieces of silver, and who ate from the same dish.
roots_summary: Hebrew cephel (H5602), a bowl or dish; tsallachath (H6747), a dish or pan, the vessel of 2 Kings 21:13; Greek trublion (G5165), a deep dish or bowl.
roots_lines: Hebrew cephel (H5602) — a bowl, a lordly dish; used of Jael's vessel and of Gideon's fleece wrung into a bowl; Judges 5:25, 6:38.
Hebrew tsallachath (H6747) — a dish, a pan; the vessel wiped and turned upside down over Jerusalem; 2 Kings 21:13, Proverbs 19:24.
Greek trublion (G5165) — a deep dish or bowl; used only of the dish in the upper room; Matthew 26:23, Mark 14:20.
usage: “She brought forth butter in a lordly dish” — the best vessel in Jael's tent.
“As a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down” — the desolation of Jerusalem in a domestic figure.
“He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish” — treachery named by the mark of favour.

pos: n. pl. (the nipples of the breast or udder; in the prophets, a figure of nourishment and, in Ezekiel, of the corruption of youth)
etymology: Old English tit, a nipple; the Authorized Version's plain agricultural word. It is used of the udders of flocks as well as of the human breast.
biblical_def: Isaiah, calling the careless women of Jerusalem to lament the coming desolation, sets the loss in agricultural terms: “They shall lament for the teats, for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine” (Isa 32:12) — the udders of the flocks, the fields, and the vines, the whole economy of nourishment failing together, and thorns and briers coming up in the land of the people. It is a lament for a country that will no longer feed its children. Ezekiel uses the same word in his hardest chapter, where Israel and Judah are drawn as two sisters whose whoredom began in Egypt in their youth (Eze 23:3, 23:21). The dictionary handles that passage soberly and does not enlarge on it: the prophet is deliberately using the language of shame to describe covenant unfaithfulness, and the shock is the sermon. What the two prophets have in common is the picture of nourishment misused or lost. Scripture's own remedy for both is the same figure turned right way up: as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby, and Isaiah 66:11 promises a Jerusalem at whose breasts her children shall be satisfied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a teat as the projecting part of the female breast; the nipple; the dug of a beast.
webster_full: TEAT, n. The projecting part of the female breast; the dug of a beast; the nipple.
2. In animals, the organ through which the young receive their nourishment.
They shall lament for the teats, for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine. Isa. xxxii.
scriptures: They shall lament for the teats, for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine.
That ye may suck, and be satisfied with the breasts of her consolations; that ye may milk out, and be delighted with the abundance of her glory.
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
corruption_summary: A generation of preaching that will not use the plain words of Scripture where Scripture uses them ends by preaching a Bible less honest about the body than the Bible is.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is an ordinary agricultural term and no one is contesting it. What is worth naming is a habit of handling on the other side: the pulpit that skips Isaiah 32, Ezekiel 16 and 23, and the Song of Solomon altogether, on the grounds that the language is indelicate. The Authorized Version is not squeamish, and neither were the prophets, because the Holy Ghost chose shocking figures on purpose. Ezekiel 23 is meant to be difficult to read aloud; that is exactly its force as a description of what covenant unfaithfulness looks like to God. A ministry that quietly edits these chapters out teaches, without ever saying so, that Scripture needs improving and that the body is a subject God handles clumsily. The right course is neither prurience nor omission but the sobriety of the text itself: read what is written, explain what it means, do not linger where the Spirit does not linger, and let the plain word do its own work. Isaiah 66:11 shows the same imagery used for pure comfort, and 1 Peter 2:2 makes the nursing infant the model of every Christian's appetite for the word.
roots_summary: Hebrew shad (H7699), the breast, the udder; dad (H1717), the breast, the teat; Greek gala (G1051), milk — the figure of 1 Peter 2:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew shad (H7699) — the breast or udder; used of the flocks' nourishment and in the divine name El Shaddai's traditional association with sufficiency; Isaiah 32:12, Genesis 49:25.
Hebrew dad (H1717) — the breast, the teat; used in Ezekiel's indictment of the sisters' youth in Egypt; Ezekiel 23:3, 23:21.
Greek gala (G1051) — milk; the sincere milk of the word by which newborn babes grow, and the elementary teaching of Hebrews 5:12; 1 Peter 2:2.
usage: “They shall lament for the teats, for the pleasant fields” — a whole economy of nourishment failing.
“Satisfied with the breasts of her consolations” — the same figure turned to comfort.
“Desire the sincere milk of the word” — the nursing infant as the model believer.
